There’s just one problem — wildfire smoke now threatens the match and FIFA, the sport’s governing body, doesn’t appear to have any plan in place to protect player or fan health. Wildfire smoke blowing from Canada has blanketed large swaths of the Midwest and East Coast in recent days, i mpacting more than a dozen states , with some of the worst-hit cities facing air quality in ranges considered hazardous. New Yorkers are among those who have been watching their air turn orange and hazy this week. On Thursday, the state issued an alert as the air quality index climbed to “unhealthy” and “ very unhealthy” levels. “Avoid spending time outdoors, if possible,” officials advised. As of Friday morning, air quality near the stadium remained in the unhealthy range, and while it’s forecast to improve to “moderate” by Sunday’s kickoff, smoke patterns could still change. If concerns continue during the finals, there’s no way to close off the open-air stadium where stars Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal are slated to square off. Here's How World Cup organizer FIFA does not appear to have any contingency plans in place for wildfire smoke. Neither FIFA nor New York City Department of Health officials immediately responded to Grist’s request for comment. In a previous statement to Grist , FIFA detailed extensive protocols related to extreme heat, including mandatory water breaks for players, but didn’t mention air quality. “Climate-related risks,” the organization wrote last month, “are assessed as part of overall tournament planning and managed in close coordination with host cities, stadium authorities, and national agencies.” Unlike FIFA, a number of other leagues implement standardized adjustments triggered by air quality warnings. Per National Women’s Soccer League policy, for instance, a women’s soccer game at Citi Field in New York on Thursday had additional hydration breaks for safety. NWSL policy adds hydration breaks at an air quality index of 101 (“unhealthy for sensitive groups”) and cancels or postpones games when the AQI tops 200 (“very unhealthy”). Major League Baseball rescheduled one game this week in Philadelphia, and Major League Soccer canceled a game in Chicago due to smoke. The World Cup is in its fifth and final week, and despite the games taking place across multiple wildfire-prone regions, so far FIFA’s bet that the air would stay clear has paid off. It may get lucky again this weekend, says Nicholas Watanabe, a professor of sport and entertainment management at the University of South Carolina, but that doesn’t excuse not being ready. completion.text:
Canada-sourced wildfire smoke that has turned skies across much of the eastern United States orange and hazy is now shadowing one of the most-watched sporting events on the calendar. Argentina and Spain are set to meet in the World Cup final on Sunday at an open-air stadium just outside New York City — a venue with no capacity to seal out compromised air — and according to [Grist](https://grist.org/extreme-weather/wildfire-smoke-threatens-the-world-cup-final-fifa-still-doesnt-have-a-plan/), the sport's governing body, FIFA, has not disclosed any contingency plan for protecting the health of players or fans if conditions deteriorate.

New York State issued an air quality alert on Thursday as the index climbed into levels classified as both "unhealthy" and "very unhealthy." Friday morning monitoring at the stadium site showed the AQI still sitting within the unhealthy band; forecasters projected an improvement to "moderate" ahead of Sunday's kickoff, though the path of smoke from active wildfires can shift on short notice. If the air remains degraded during the final, players and fans in that exposed setting could experience burning throats, coughing, or headaches — symptoms that carry elevated risk for children, older spectators, and anyone with a respiratory condition such as asthma.

Spain's national team held an outdoor practice in New Jersey on Thursday even as those state alerts were active. Dr. Courtney Howard, an emergency room physician and official with the Global Climate and Health Alliance, told the Associated Press that elite athletes working under those conditions face a compounded danger: "These are high-level athletes who are moving a lot of air through their lungs. They shouldn't be practicing outside if the air quality levels are at hazardous sort of ranges for wildfire-related air pollution."

## FIFA Has No Smoke Playbook

FIFA has not responded to questions from [Grist](https://grist.org/extreme-weather/wildfire-smoke-threatens-the-world-cup-final-fifa-still-doesnt-have-a-plan/) about its air quality protocols, nor has the New York City Department of Health. In a prior statement to the outlet, FIFA outlined detailed heat-management procedures — mandatory water breaks among them — but made no mention of air quality. The organization's stated position, provided to Grist last month, is that "climate-related risks are assessed as part of overall tournament planning and managed in close coordination with host cities, stadium authorities, and national agencies."

Other major leagues operating under the same smoke conditions this week have not waited for the air to clear before adjusting play. The National Women's Soccer League mandates additional hydration breaks once the air quality index reaches 101 — the "unhealthy for sensitive groups" threshold — and cancels or postpones fixtures when the index tops 200. A Thursday NWSL match at Citi Field in New York proceeded under those supplemental break provisions. Major League Baseball shifted a Philadelphia game off its original date because of smoke, and Major League Soccer canceled a Chicago fixture entirely.

The contrast has not gone unobserved. Trinity Rodman, who took part in that Citi Field match while smoke hung over the city, distilled the underlying tension in a single observation: "If we have to have a hydration break every 15 minutes, then we shouldn't be playing the game," she said, as reported by [Grist](https://grist.org/extreme-weather/wildfire-smoke-threatens-the-world-cup-final-fifa-still-doesnt-have-a-plan/). The NWSL's own rules effectively treat that break interval as the marker for conditions too severe to continue — a standard the World Cup carries no equivalent of.

## A Tournament-Long Bet That Has, So Far, Held

The 2026 World Cup enters its fifth and final week having staged matches across multiple regions of the United States where wildfire risk is a documented and recurring feature of summer. Grist reports that FIFA's approach throughout has amounted to an assumption that the air would cooperate. That assumption had not been seriously tested until this week.

Nicholas Watanabe, a professor of sport and entertainment management at the University of South Carolina, told Grist that running out the clock on favorable conditions does not substitute for preparation. "FIFA seems unprepared for these wildfires," he said. "At the same time, it looks like the worst of the pollution will dissipate before the World Cup Final, so FIFA will dodge a bullet and likely push forward with the match."

Climate-driven disruptions to elite sport have accumulated across multiple disciplines this summer. Competitors in the Tour de France have contended with wildfire smoke and extreme heat throughout the current edition of that event. Yellow jersey holder Tadej Pogačar, asked about the conditions, suggested the entire racing calendar needs rethinking: "I would change the whole calendar," he said earlier this month. He added, pointedly: "It's not something I can do." Scheduling authority rests with governing bodies, not athletes — a structural fact that frames what FIFA's inaction on air quality actually means in practice.

Watanabe argued that a near-miss, even one that causes no measurable harm to players or fans on Sunday, should accelerate institutional change. "Hopefully," he said, "this is a wakeup call to FIFA and all other sport leagues and competitions of the need for regulations and a comprehensive plan to deal with climate risks."

Whether the final is ultimately spared remains open as of this writing. The stadium cannot be closed, the forecast carries acknowledged uncertainty, and FIFA has not described any threshold at which it would alter or suspend play because of air quality. Those facts hold regardless of what the index reads at kickoff Sunday.

"Hopefully," he said, "this is a wakeup call to FIFA and all other sport leagues and competitions of the need for regulations and a comprehensive plan to deal with climate risks."

Whether the final is ultimately spared remains open as of this writing. The stadium cannot be closed, the forecast carries acknowledged uncertainty, and FIFA has not described any threshold at which it would alter or suspend play because of air quality. Those facts hold regardless of what the index reads at kickoff Sunday.
